Daniel usefully shifts the discussion from “human agency” to the real workhorse of many causal designs—*independence between treatment assignment and potential outcomes*—but he risks replacing one muddle with another. In the Rubin/Fisher tradition, randomization is valuable not because it injects metaphysical “free will,” but because it makes assignment *as-if independent* of the confounders we worry about, given what we can observe and justify ([Rubin causal model](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rubin_causal_model); [Fisher’s randomization logic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randomized_experiment)). That’s an epistemic claim about information and design, not an ontological claim about whether the world is deterministic. If “every other human is predictable,” their trials could still be credible provided the assignment mechanism is verifiably decoupled from the outcome-generating factors (e.g., a precommitted algorithm, physical randomizer, or administrative lottery). Conversely, a “free” human can still assign treatment in a confounded way.

The deeper blind spot is the equation of “studying causality” with “having an independent source of randomness.” Randomization is sufficient for many causal questions, but not necessary: causal identification can also come from structural knowledge, instruments, regression discontinuities, panel designs, or other assumptions that do not require literal randomness—only credible constraints on how the treatment is generated and how variables relate ([Pearl’s interventionist framing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Causality_(book))). Daniel’s final sentence gestures at a profound limit—if some hidden variable correlates with *every* apparent randomizer, no experiment can break confounding—but stated that strongly it collapses into a superdeterminist worry where *no* empirical method works. If that is the point, the post should say so explicitly; if not, it would help to reframe “independent randomness” as “an assignment mechanism plausibly independent of the relevant potential outcomes, conditional on the design,” which is a demanding standard—but one that doesn’t require metaphysical claims about agency or unpredictability.
